title: Why are clocks dropping the leap second?

record.question: Why did the world's timekeepers vote to stop adding leap seconds, and what happens instead?
record.audience_reason: Every phone, bank and GPS receiver depends on UTC; the October 2026 vote is a once-in-50-years change to how the world tells time, and it's a follow-up to our time-zones episode.

editorial_contribution.statement: We run atom time and Earth time side by side for the whole episode, show with a labeled calculation how milliseconds per day become a second in about a year, animate the real 27-step IERS leap-second record (9 in the 1970s, none since 2016), explain why a speeding-up Earth made a first-ever negative leap second a risk, and reveal the new limit (0.9 s to 1 hour) on a labeled log scale.

record.custom_scene: Split panels for the whole episode: a cesium atom and digital clock (left), Earth from above the pole turning under the sun (right), with a yellow gap bar as the through-line; a 2.7 ms/day calendar fill; a clock ticking into 23:59:60 while the gap gauge snaps back; the real TAI-UTC staircase 1972-2017; a negative leap second skipping :59; the allowed gap zooming from 0.9 s to one hour on a log axis.

cover_composition.main_object: atom panel and Earth panel with a gap between them

record.sources_and_assumptions: See sources-and-rights.md. The 2.7 ms/day figure is a labeled illustration, not a measured average. The decade count and dates come from the IERS table. The 30% figure is the CCTF/IERS workshop estimate quoted in Resolution 5.
record.asset_provenance: All visuals drawn in code; IERS leap-second dates from IANA tzdata leap-seconds.list (public domain data); Inter (OFL); DejaVu Sans Mono; narration Kokoro (Apache-2.0); sound effects synthesized.

scenes.subject: two panels: atom clock ticking; Earth turning under the sun; a yellow gap opens between them

explain.understand: there are two kinds of time and they differ
explain.cause: the two clocks run at different rates

scenes.tts: Your phone keeps time with atoms. The sun keeps time with a spinning planet. And the two don't agree.
scenes.caption: Your phone keeps time with atoms.|The sun keeps time with a spinning planet.|And the two don't agree.

scenes.subject: even atom ticks (left) vs uneven Earth-day ticks (right); tides and interior labels

explain.understand: atomic seconds are constant; Earth's day length varies
explain.cause: tidal drag and shifts inside Earth

scenes.tts: An atomic second never changes. Earth's spin does. Tides from the Moon drag on it, and shifts deep inside the planet nudge it faster or slower.
scenes.caption: An atomic second never changes.|Earth's spin does.|Tides from the Moon drag on it,|and shifts deep inside the planet|nudge it faster or slower.

scenes.subject: illustrative calculation: calendar squares fill for 370 days; gap bar reaches one second
changes: days count to 370 while the gap bar fills to 1.00 s

explain.understand: milliseconds per day accumulate to a second in about a year

scenes.tts: Tiny gaps pile up. Say every day ran 2.7 thousandths of a second long. After about a year, Earth would be a full second behind the atoms.
scenes.caption: Tiny gaps pile up.|Say every day ran 2.7 thousandths of a second long.|After about a year,|Earth would be a full second behind the atoms.

scenes.subject: UTC clock counts 23:59:58 → 23:59:60 → 00:00:00; gap gauge climbs to 0.9 s and snaps back
changes: gauge climbs toward the 0.9 s line

explain.understand: a leap second resets the gap
objects: gap gauge with 0 and 0.9 s lines
explain.change: an extra second is shown and the gap falls
explain.cause: the inserted second lets Earth catch up

scenes.tts: So timekeepers built a patch. Whenever the gap neared nine-tenths of a second, they added one. The clock read 23:59:60.
scenes.caption: So timekeepers built a patch.|Whenever the gap neared nine-tenths of a second,|they added one.|The clock read 23:59:60.

scenes.subject: real IERS data: TAI-UTC staircase from 10 s to 37 s, 1972-2017; 1970s highlighted
changes: last step marked on 'New Year's Eve'
scenes.tts: Since 1972, they've done it 27 times. Nine in the 1970s alone. The last one landed on New Year's Eve, 2016.
scenes.caption: Since 1972, they've done it 27 times.|Nine in the 1970s alone.|The last one landed on New Year's Eve, 2016.

scenes.subject: Earth spinning faster with yellow speed arcs; a negative leap second deleting :59; 30% odds chip

explain.understand: a faster Earth raised the odds of the first negative leap second

scenes.tts: Then Earth sped up. Recent years brought the shortest days atomic clocks have ever measured. That raised a scary first: deleting a second. Timekeepers put the odds at thirty percent by 2035.
scenes.caption: Then Earth sped up.|Recent years brought the shortest days|atomic clocks have ever measured.|That raised a scary first: deleting a second.|Timekeepers put the odds at thirty percent by 2035.

scenes.subject: scale reveal: the allowed gap zooms out from 0.9 s to one hour on a log axis
changes: axis zooms out and the yellow bar runs to 1 hour on 'an hour'

explain.understand: the new rule allows a gap 4,000 times larger, so no patch for centuries

scenes.tts: So in October, the world's timekeepers voted to stop patching. From May 20th, 2027, the clocks just keep counting. The gap with Earth can grow to as much as an hour.
scenes.caption: So in October, the world's timekeepers|voted to stop patching.|From May 20th, 2027, the clocks just keep counting.|The gap with Earth can grow|to as much as an hour.

scenes.subject: phone and sun panels side by side, a thin gap allowed to drift
scenes.tts: So here's the new deal. Your phone counts atoms. The sun follows the spin. From 2027, they're allowed to disagree... by up to an hour. Follow for one bonus braincell per scroll.
scenes.caption: So here's the new deal.|Your phone counts atoms.|The sun follows the spin.|From 2027, they're allowed to disagree...|by up to an hour.|Follow for one bonus braincell per scroll.
